title: Sagas
summary: Sagas replace distributed atomicity with sequenced local transactions plus compensations — how they work, fail, and when to use them.

blocks.title: The one idea that matters
blocks.text: A Saga does **not give you atomicity**. It gives you **eventual consistency without holding locks across services** by committing each step locally and undoing completed steps with explicit compensating actions when something later fails. If you remember nothing else: **forward commit, backward compensate, never block.**

A Saga is a sequence of **local transactions `T1, T2, ..., Tn`**, each owned by a different service and committed in its own database, plus a defined **compensating transaction `C1, C2, ..., Ck`** for every step that has a semantic undo. If all `Ti` succeed, the Saga succeeds. If `Tj` fails, you run compensations in **reverse order `C(j-1) ... C1`** to semantically undo what already committed. There is no global lock, no prepare phase, no shared transaction log. Each service guarantees only its own ACID properties; the Saga as a whole guarantees only that you end in either a fully completed state or a fully compensated state — with a long, visible window in between where the system is **partially complete and observable to other readers**.

You reach for this because **two-phase commit (2PC) does not survive service autonomy**. 2PC requires every participant to hold locks and promise to commit on command from a coordinator. That means synchronous availability coupling — if one participant is slow or down, everyone blocks — plus lock contention that kills throughput, plus a coordinator that becomes a single point of failure and a deployment bottleneck when teams own separate databases, schemas, and release cycles. Sagas accept the trade-off explicitly: **give up isolation to keep availability, autonomy, and independent evolution**. The cost is application-level complexity: you must design every undo, tolerate dirty reads, and handle a compensation that itself can fail.

In **orchestration**, one controller — a saga orchestrator or the originating service — issues commands, tracks state, and decides to proceed or compensate. The logic lives in one place: `reserve payment -> reserve inventory -> book shipment`, and on failure the orchestrator walks backward. Choose this when the flow is complex, has branching, or needs centralized timeouts and retries, because debugging is dramatically easier. The trade-off is coupling to the orchestrator and load concentration — it must be stateful, durable, and highly available, otherwise every in-flight saga dies with it.

In **choreography**, there is no controller. Each service publishes domain events and the next service reacts: `OrderCreated -> PaymentReserved -> InventoryReserved -> Shipped`, with failure events triggering listeners that compensate locally. Choose this for simple linear flows with stable service topology, because it removes a central bottleneck and keeps services decoupled. The trade-off is **emergent behavior**: the end-to-end flow exists nowhere in code, so adding a step, changing order, or answering *where is order 42 stuck?* requires tracing events across logs. Most production pain I have seen comes from teams picking choreography for a flow that was actually complex and then drowning in event spaghetti.

blocks.title: Compensation is not rollback
blocks.text: A database rollback restores old values and is invisible. A compensation is a **new business action with side effects** — refund, cancel, restock, send correction email. It can fail, it can be partial, and the outside world already saw the intermediate state. Design it as a first-class operation, not an `except: rollback()` afterthought.

This is the part candidates hand-wave and interviewers pounce on. Because `T1` commits before `T2` runs, other transactions **see dirty intermediate state**: inventory looks reserved before payment clears, seats look booked before fraud check finishes. You cannot prevent this with the saga pattern itself. You mitigate it three ways, each with a cost. One, **semantic locks**: mark the entity as `PENDING` so concurrent readers treat it as unavailable — simple, but you just reintroduced contention at the application layer. Two, **commutativity and last-writer-wins design**: make operations order-tolerant so temporary overshoot is acceptable and corrected later — works for counters and carts, fails for non-fungible resources like the last airline seat. Three, **pessimistic reservation with expiry**: hold a short TTL reservation that auto-releases — bounds the anomaly window but requires a reaper and clock discipline. Name which one you picked and why; *no isolation* is not an answer.

blocks.caption: Saga vs two-phase commit, stated honestly.
rows: Atomicity
No. Intermediate states visible. Ends compensated, not as if never happened.
Yes. All commit or all abort, no visible partial state.
Isolation
None across services. Must handle dirty reads in app logic.
Strong. Locks held until global decision.
Availability
High. Each step proceeds independently; failed steps compensate asynchronously.
Low. All participants block on coordinator; one slow node stalls all.
Latency / throughput
High throughput, no distributed locks. More messages for compensations.
Lock hold time grows with slowest participant; throughput collapses under contention.
Complexity
In application code: idempotent compensations, state machine, observability.
In infrastructure: coordinator HA, recovery log, blocking failure handling.

blocks.text: How it fails in production, and the symptom you would see

Sagas do not fail cleanly — they get **stuck halfway** in ways that page you at 3am. The classic killers: a **non-compensatable step** executes and then a later step fails — you charged the card, the warehouse step timed out, and there is no automatic undo for *shipped a physical box*, so you need human intervention. A **compensation fails** — refund API returns `500` three times, message broker drops the `ReleaseInventory` event, and you now hold money and stock forever. **Lost saga state** — the orchestrator crashed without persisting its cursor, so on restart it re-issues `T2` and double-reserves. **Out-of-order or duplicate events** in choreography cause a compensation to run before its forward step completes, or twice. Every one of these is a direct consequence of the core trade-off: you removed the coordinator lock, so correctness now depends on **durable state, idempotency, and retry discipline** that you must build yourself.

items: **Money moved but order shows failed:** payment `T1` committed, inventory `T2` timed out ambiguously, compensation `C1` never ran or failed silently. Check for missing idempotency keys and dead-lettered refund messages.
**Inventory leak / phantom reservations:** `ReleaseInventory` lost or applied out of order. Reservations with no TTL pile up, available-to-promise drifts to zero while the warehouse is half empty.
**Duplicate side effects:** customer charged twice, two shipment labels created. Symptom of orchestrator retry without idempotent receivers — same command delivered twice, both executed.
**Zombie sagas stuck in COMPENSATING for hours:** one compensation keeps failing and blocks the rest because you compensated strictly sequentially without a retry backoff plus escalation path.

**Inconsistent read anomalies reported by support:** user saw *order confirmed* then *order cancelled* minutes later. Not a bug — it is saga isolation semantics surfacing. Fix is UX and semantic `PENDING` state, not stronger consistency.

blocks.title: Saga execution state machine
blocks.caption: Compensating is a durable state, not a transient catch block.
blocks.code:
stateDiagram-v2
  [*] --> Active
  Active --> Completed: all Ti succeeded
  Active --> Compensating: Tj failed or timed out
  Compensating --> Compensated: all Ck succeeded
  Compensating --> Stuck: compensation failed after retries
  Stuck --> Compensating: retry or manual fix
  Stuck --> Escalated: alert human workflow

blocks.text: The code looks trivial and that is the trap. Three decisions carry all the weight. First, **durable cursor before next call**: `store.append` must be flushed before invoking the next service, otherwise a crash causes double-execution or a skipped compensation — you traded a distributed lock for a local write-ahead log, so make that log bulletproof. Second, **idempotency keys on every forward and compensation** (`saga_id:step_index`): without them retries are unsafe and at-least-once delivery becomes double-charge. Third, **compensations are enqueued, not called inline**: a compensation that throws must go to a durable retry queue with backoff and eventual human escalation, never bubble up and vanish. If your compensation path is `try/except: log.error`, you do not have a saga — you have a hope.

blocks.title: Check compensatability first
blocks.text: Before drawing any saga, list each step as **compensatable, retryable, or pivot**. The pivot is the point of no return (e.g., *dispatch courier*). Everything after the pivot cannot be undone — you must go forward with retries and human workflow. If a step is neither compensatable nor retryable, **do not put it in a saga**.
How it shows up in interview

items.title: You get a multi-service write
items.text: Design order checkout, travel booking, or money transfer across services. The interviewer wants you to reject distributed transactions explicitly and propose sagas with reasons, not jump to events.

items.title: Orchestration vs choreography choice
items.text: Say which one and defend it. Good answer: orchestration for complex checkout with timeouts and visibility; choreography only for simple linear pipelines. Mention the debuggability trade-off.

items.title: Define compensations concretely
items.text: For every forward step, name the exact compensation: `reserve -> release`, `charge -> refund`, `book -> cancel with fee`. Flag any non-compensatable step and propose a pivot plus manual process.

items.title: Handle the nasty properties
items.text: Bring up idempotency keys, durable orchestrator state, retry with backoff, out-of-order events, and dirty reads with `PENDING` states — before being asked. This is where medium becomes hire.

items.title: Close with failure and observability
items.text: Explain stuck-saga detection, dead-letter queues, saga audit trail per ID, and alerting on `COMPENSATING` age. Interviewers grade whether your saga is operable, not just drawable.

items: **Sagas are ACID across services** — false. They provide atomicity of outcome only after compensations settle, with no isolation. Anyone claiming *rollback* does not understand the pattern.

**Choreography is always more decoupled and therefore better** — false. It decouples runtime but couples evolution: changing step order requires touching every publisher and subscriber, and end-to-end reasoning is lost.

**Compensations always succeed** — the most dangerous assumption. Compensations call real APIs that fail, so they need their own retries, idempotency, and escalation. A saga without a `Stuck` state is incomplete.
**Exactly-once messaging solves sagas** — there is no exactly-once across services. You get at-least-once plus idempotent handlers. Design for duplicates from day one.

**Sagas replace all consistency needs** — they do not fix reads. If the business cannot tolerate *confirmed then cancelled*, you need a different boundary: co-locate the data, use a reservation pattern, or admit the UX must expose pending state.

blocks.text: When to use it and when not to

blocks.caption: Use sagas for autonomous multi-service writes; avoid them when you can avoid distribution.
headers: Do NOT use a Saga when
rows: Write spans 2+ services/databases owned by different teams with independent deploys.
All data can live in one database — use a local ACID transaction instead. Simpler and strictly stronger.
Business can tolerate temporary inconsistency and a visible PENDING state (e-commerce, booking, provisioning).
Business requires immediate strong consistency (last seat, ledger balance check) — co-locate or use reservations + synchronous check.
Every step has a defined compensation or a clear pivot with manual fallback.
A step is irreversible with no business remedy — e.g., firing a missile, sending an immutable legal filing.
Long-lived flow with timeouts, human steps, or third-party calls that cannot hold DB locks.
Short, low-latency, high-contention update where lock hold time is tiny and 2PC cost is acceptable — rare, but real inside one trust domain.

blocks.title: What to say in one sentence if asked
blocks.text: **Use a saga when a business process spans autonomous services: commit each step locally for availability, and on failure run idempotent compensations in reverse order — accepting temporary inconsistency to avoid distributed locks.**
